To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) in the absence of fatty acid binding protein mitochondrial Ca2+ transport is affected by fatty acids and their derivatives, and 2) in the presence of fatty acid binding proteins, mitochondrial Ca2+ transpo is protected against the adverse effects of fatty acids and their intermediates.
the accumulation of lipid metabolite, such as fatty acid, fatty acyl-coenzyme A and acylcarmite, in the ishemic myocardium may be responsible for disturbance of mitochondrial calcium fluxes.
the effects of fatty acid metabolites on mitochondrial Ca2+-fluxes are reversed by albumin, an intracellular fatty-acid-binding protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of fatty acid metabolites in the ischaemia-reperfusion injury.
the effects of lipid metabolites on mitochondrial Ca2+, and the possible involvement of an intracellular binding protein in these effects.
the role of fatty acid derivatives in ischaemia/reperfusion injury.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fatty acids and their derivatives, which accumulate in the ischaemically injured myocardial cell, do not directly affect the mitochondrial Ca2+ handling system.

the accumulation of fatty acid derivatives, such as fatty acid, acyl-CoAs and acylcarmite, in the ischamic myocardial cell, does not necessarily lead to a disturbance in mitochondrial Ca2 fluxes, but rather depends on the presence of an avid intracellular fatty acid binder.
fatty acid derivatives are capable of affecting mitochondrial Ca2+ handling and that these effects can be reversed in the presence of an albumin-like intracellular protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the accumulation of fatty acid metabolites in the ischaemia myocardium, may lead to a disturbance in mitochondrial Ca2+-handling.
the accumulation of free fatty acids in the ischaemized heart does not lead to an increase in mitochondrial Ca2+-uptake and Ca2+-release.
fatty acids and their derivatives, such as acyl-CoA, acylcarnitin and acylphospholipid, have a direct inhibitory effect on the mitochondrial Ca2+ cycle, which is reversed by the presence of albumin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fatty acid derivatives, such as fatty acyl-CoAs, acylcarnitin and free fatty acids, may be involved in the regulation of mitochondrial Ca2+ homeostasis.
the presence of albumin in the medium reverses the inhibitory effects of fatty acids, fatty acid derivatives and fatty acid binding protein on mitochondrial Ca2 + transport.
fatty acids, acetyl-CoA, and acylcarna- itines, all of which are present in high concentrations during ischaemia, can alter the Ca2+ handling of cardiac mitochondria.
